questions.stem: Madhubani painting, recognised as a GI-tagged folk art, originates from which Indian region?

options.option_text: Mithila region of Bihar (Madhubani district especially)

questions.explanation: Madhubani / Mithila painting — Madhubani district + Darbhanga region, Bihar. Traditionally done by women on mud walls + floors of homes; now also on paper, cloth. Themes — Hindu deities (Ram-Sita, Krishna), nature, social events. Distinct features: bright natural colours (turmeric, indigo, soot), no empty space (filled with floral / animal motifs), double outlines, fish + sun + moon symbols. GI tag 2007. Sita Devi (Padma Shri) revived it in the 1960s. Bharti Dayal, Mahasundari Devi — other notable artists.

questions.stem: Warli painting — characterised by a distinctive use of basic geometric shapes (circles, triangles, squares) and stick-figures depicting daily life — is from:

options.option_text: Maharashtra (Warli tribe of the Sahyadri / Western Ghats foothills, Thane / Palghar)

questions.explanation: Warli — Maharashtra; Warli tribe of Thane + Palghar districts (also Dadra & Nagar Haveli). One of the oldest tribal art forms (claimed to date back to ~3000 BCE in some traditions; modern revival from the 1970s — Jivya Soma Mashe (Padma Shri 2011) was the trailblazer). DISTINCTIVE STYLE — only WHITE PIGMENT (rice-paste) on RED-OCHRE wall background; NO COLOUR. Geometric forms: circle = sun/moon, triangle = mountains/trees, square = sacred enclosure (chauk). Tarpa dance, marriage rituals, harvest scenes. GI tag 2014. Now widely commercialised — featured in fashion, corporate murals.

questions.stem: Pattachitra — a traditional cloth-based scroll painting characterised by intricate detailing — is associated primarily with:

options.option_text: Odisha (Raghurajpur is the heritage village) and West Bengal

questions.explanation: Pattachitra — Sanskrit 'patta' (cloth) + 'chitra' (picture). Origins ~12th century, in service of Jagannath Temple, Puri (the deities themselves are 'painted' annually). Themes — Jagannath, Vishnu's avatars, Ramayana, Mahabharata. Rich colours from natural pigments (conch shell white, lamp soot black, hingul red). Intricate borders. Heritage village — Raghurajpur (Puri district). Bengal Pattachitra — narrative scrolls (jadupata) used by traditional storytellers; longer, more linear. GI tag — Odia Pattachitra (2008). Notable masters: Jagannath Mahapatra, Bhagat Mahapatra.

questions.stem: Kalamkari painting / printing — using natural dyes and bamboo pens — has two main schools, both in which state?
questions.explanation: Kalamkari — Persian 'kalam' (pen) + 'kari' (work) → 'pen-craft'. Two distinct schools in AP: (1) SRIKALAHASTI (Chittoor district) — religious / mythological themes (Ramayana, Krishna leelas); strictly hand-drawn with bamboo/tamarind pen. (2) MACHILIPATNAM (Krishna district) — block-printed; floral patterns, Persian motifs (legacy of trade with Iran via Golconda); more secular use. 17 steps using vegetable dyes — myrobalan, indigo, turmeric, pomegranate. GI tag — Srikalahasti 2008, Machilipatnam 2009. Recently popular in fashion (sarees, dupattas, kurtas). Pedana — village in Machilipatnam known for the cluster.

questions.stem: Phad painting — long horizontal scrolls used as portable temples by traditional 'Bhopa' singer-priests — is from:
questions.explanation: Phad — Rajasthan; ~700 years old. Long horizontal cloth scrolls (~30 ft long, ~5 ft tall) depicting heroic ballads of folk deities — PABUJI (cattle-warrior, most popular) and DEVNARAYAN. Bhopa-Bhopis (priest-singers + their wives) carry the rolled-up Phad village to village; perform overnight all-night narrations using a lamp + ravanhatta (string instrument). Made by Joshi family (Shahpura, Bhilwara). Brushes are squirrel-hair; colours are vegetable + mineral. GI tag 2018. Other Rajasthan painting forms: Pichwai (Nathdwara, Krishna devotional cloth backings), Mandana (mud-wall floor / wall art by women).

questions.stem: Tanjore (Thanjavur) painting — rich, devotional, with raised gesso-work and gold-leaf embellishment — flourished under whose patronage?

options.option_text: Maratha kings of Tanjore (post-1676; especially Sarfoji-II), continuing earlier Vijayanagara traditions

questions.explanation: Tanjore painting — Tamil Nadu, Thanjavur. Patronised by the Maratha rulers of Thanjavur (the Bhonsle dynasty, 1676-1855, after Maratha forces under Venkoji = Shivaji's half-brother captured Thanjavur). King Sarfoji II (r. 1798-1832) — major patron. Earlier roots in Vijayanagara + Nayakas of Madurai. Distinct features: WOODEN PANELS, RAISED GESSO WORK (using chalk paste — like 3D embossing), real GOLD LEAF, semi-precious stones embedded, vivid colours. Themes — Krishna (especially Bal-Krishna), goddesses, Hindu mythology. GI tag 2007-08. Mysore painting (Karnataka) is a sister style — also gold + gesso, but flatter, more delicate.

questions.stem: Pithora painting — ritual wall art associated with the Rathwa, Bhilala and Nayaka tribes, often depicting horses — is from:

options.option_text: Gujarat (Chhota Udepur) and Madhya Pradesh (Jhabua) tribal belt

questions.explanation: Pithora painting — tribal ritual mural art. Done on the inner walls of homes during important ceremonies (marriages, vows). Central motif — horses (the deity Pithoro / Pithora Dev, mount of the local creator god Baba Pithora). Scenes of village life, hunting, planting. Done by hereditary 'Lakhara' painters; takes 3 days; involves prescribed rituals. Region — Chhota Udepur (Gujarat), Jhabua, Alirajpur (MP), and adjoining Bhil-tribal areas. Other tribal painting traditions in India: SAURA (Odisha tribe — close to Warli style); GOND (Madhya Pradesh — Jangarh Singh Shyam revived it in modern art form); CHITRAKAR / PATUA (Bengal scroll-painters); CHERIYAL scrolls (Telangana); KOHBAR (Bihar — bridal-chamber walls).
